content: The transfusion of red blood cells (RBCs) is a widely used treatment for anemia across various medical conditions. A key concern in clinical practice is whether the duration of RBC storage before transfusion impacts patient outcomes. RBCs can be stored for up to 42 days, and understanding the effects of storage duration is critical for both clinical decision-making and blood bank inventory management. To evaluate this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted comparing the transfusion of RBCs stored for shorter durations versus longer durations, as well as shorter durations versus standard practice durations. A systematic review included 22 trials with a total of 42,835 participants. The quality of evidence for the primary outcome, which was in-hospital and short-term mortality, ranged from very low to moderate. Transfusion of RBCs Stored for Shorter Versus Longer Durations Eleven trials involving 2,249 participants compared RBCs stored for shorter versus longer durations. These trials included diverse populations: low birth weight neonates, children with severe anemia due to malaria or sickle cell disease, and adults in various clinical settings such as intensive care, cardiac surgery, and major elective surgery. Only two trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, while most had unclear risks in multiple domains. In adults undergoing major elective cardiac or non-cardiac surgery, transfusion of RBCs stored for shorter durations likely results in little to no difference in mortality at seven days (risk ratio [RR] 1.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 3.06; moderate-quality evidence) or at 30 days (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.45; moderate-quality evidence). For neonates, no studies reported on in-hospital or short-term mortality. At 40 weeks gestational age, the effect of shorter versus longer storage duration on mortality was uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.85; 1 trial, 52 participants). In children with severe anemia, the effect of shorter versus longer storage duration on mortality was also uncertain within 24 hours of transfusion (RR 1.50, 95% CI 0.43 to 5.25; very low-quality evidence) or at 30 days (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.45 to 4.31; low-quality evidence). Adverse transfusion reactions were reported in only one trial involving children with severe anemia. In this trial, one child in each group experienced an adverse reaction within 24 hours of transfusion. Transfusion of RBCs Stored for Shorter Versus Standard Practice Durations Eleven trials involving 40,588 participants compared RBCs stored for shorter durations versus standard practice durations. These trials included critically ill term neonates (three trials, two of which involved very low birth weight neonates) and critically ill or non-critically ill adults (eight trials, most of whom were hospitalized). Four trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the others had unclear risks in multiple domains. In adults, transfusion of RBCs stored for shorter durations likely results in little to no difference in in-hospital mortality (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.14; moderate-quality evidence), ICU mortality (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.15; moderate-quality evidence), or 30-day mortality (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.13; moderate-quality evidence). Among neonates, two trials reported no adverse transfusion reactions, while one trial reported a single case of cytomegalovirus infection in the standard practice storage group. In critically ill adults, two trials reported on transfusion reactions. One trial found no difference in acute transfusion reactions between groups (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.36), while the other observed more febrile non-hemolytic reactions in the shorter storage duration group (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.95). Conclusions Large, high-quality RCTs, primarily in adults, have shown no evidence that the duration of RBC storage affects mortality. However, the quality of evidence for neonates and children remains low. Current blood bank practices, which prioritize the use of the oldest available RBCs, can continue safely. While additional RCTs are not necessary, future research using alternative study designs should focus on specific subgroups, such as patients requiring multiple RBC units, and on factors influencing RBC quality.
